name: Fuel cell
summary: An electrochemical source that converts hydrogen or another fuel directly into DC electricity, usually followed by a converter.
description: A fuel cell produces DC electricity from an electrochemical reaction between a fuel, usually hydrogen, and oxygen from air. Unlike a battery it does not store its reactants; it runs as long as fuel is supplied. Stack voltage falls noticeably with load current, so a DC/DC converter or inverter almost always follows it.

Drawings show the cell or stack as a rectangle with plates, or as a cell symbol labelled FC, with positive and negative DC leads. Balance-of-plant items such as the air blower, humidifier and coolant pump are auxiliary loads and normally appear on a separate auxiliary supply drawing.

The symbol does not state whether the stack can follow fast load changes. Most fuel cell systems pair with a battery or supercapacitor to cover transients, and the fuel supply, purge and safety interlocks belong on the process drawings.
readingNotes: Expect a converter and often a battery buffer next to the stack.
Separate stack output from auxiliary consumption when reading ratings.
drawingChecklist: State stack voltage range and current.
Reference fuel supply and safety interlocks.
distinction: A fuel cell converts supplied fuel continuously; a battery stores a fixed charge and must be recharged.
